content: 1. Health Technology Assessments (HTAs) are often requested by procurement agencies, public healthcare providers, or national regulatory agencies. However, a significant number of respondents reported that requests for HTAs never or almost never originated from organizations outside the Ministry of Health. 2. Professionals involved in the preparation of HTA reports and decision-making include public health experts (epidemiologists, biostatisticians, health economists, and public health professionals), clinical scientists (medical doctors, nurses, pharmacists, and health professional organizations), bioethicists, sociologists, legal experts, engineers, and information specialists. Civil society and patient representatives also contribute by addressing consumer needs. 3. About half of the respondents indicated that personnel involved in preparing HTA reports were required to declare conflicts of interest, with this requirement being most common in the European Region (EUR). Similarly, HTA outcomes and subsequent policy decisions were made public in approximately half of the responding countries. 4. In most countries, findings from HTA-related organizations played an advisory rather than mandatory role in policy decisions. However, the extent to which these findings influenced final decisions remains unclear. 5. Barriers to strengthening HTA capacity were reported across all regions. These included a lack of funding (reported by 77 countries), insufficient information (59 countries), and limited knowledge of HTA methodologies (58 countries). Respondents from 65 countries suggested that raising awareness about the importance of HTA could improve its integration into decision-making processes. 6. Fewer than half of the responding countries had academic or training programs to build HTA capacity. This lack of training infrastructure was identified as a major barrier to increasing the use of HTA. Internal staff training sessions or external courses, seminars, and workshops were conducted in about half of the countries. 7. Most countries reported having a process for collecting and analyzing information about health technologies or interventions and assessing their impact. However, only a few explicitly referred to this process as HTA. 8. Two-thirds of the countries reported having a national HTA organization, department, unit, or committee that produced HTA reports for the Ministry of Health. Most countries also reported having more than six staff members in their HTA units, agencies, or committees. 9. HTAs in most responding countries primarily focused on safety and clinical effectiveness, followed by economic and budgetary considerations. Ethical, equity, and feasibility issues received little attention. 10. Ministries of Health or national health insurance bodies were the primary initiators of most HTAs. Public health professionals and clinical science experts were commonly involved in HTA preparation and decision-making. Civil society representatives were allowed to comment on HTA recommendations in half of the countries. 11. The lack of qualified human resources was identified as the main barrier to producing and using HTA. Most countries lacked academic or training programs to build HTA capacity. 12. The World Health Organization (WHO) will continue to raise awareness, promote knowledge, and encourage the practice of HTA and its use in evidence-informed decision-making. The 2015 Global Survey on HTA provides the first systematic description of HTA-related work carried out by national or government institutions in WHO Member States. 13. WHO urges Member States to establish national systems for HTA, strengthen the link between HTA and regulation, develop national methodological guidelines, and promote HTA within national frameworks. Member States are also encouraged to collaborate regionally and internationally to share information, build capacity, and implement evidence-based health policies. 14. WHO requests the Director-General to assess the status of HTA in Member States, raise awareness, foster knowledge, and encourage the practice of HTA among national policymakers and other stakeholders.
